title: The harm of backbiting
hookLine: mentioning your brother with what he'd dislike (Muslim)

lines: DO YOU KNOW WHAT IT IS?
cards: Do you know what backbiting is? The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, put that question to his companions, and Sahih Muslim records it.
They answered the way people answer a teacher they trust: Allah and his Messenger know best. So he told them. Backbiting is mentioning your brother with something he would dislike.
Then someone asked the question group chats ask sooner or later. But what if it's true? What if I'm only saying what he really did?
Today: the harm of backbiting, and the answer.

teach.h: IF IT'S TRUE, IT'S STILL BACKBITING.
teach.b: If what you say about him is true, that is backbiting. If it isn't true, that's something else, buhtan, slander. So truth isn't a defense here; truth is the definition.
The test is whether he'd dislike hearing it said behind his back. Second, the Qur'an's picture, a hard one, first met on day five hundred eighty-seven.

teach.h: THE FLESH OF A DEAD BROTHER.
teach.b: In Pickthall's words: "neither backbite one another. Would one of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother? Ye abhor that". The image is meant to turn the stomach.
Some readers notice a detail: the dead can't answer back, and neither can someone who isn't in the room. Third, the honest exceptions.
Scholars such as an-Nawawi listed cases where naming someone's fault is allowed: asking for help against a wrong done to you, seeking a ruling, warning someone about a real danger.
In a hadith in al-Bukhari, a woman named Hind told the Prophet that her husband didn't give her enough to live on, and he answered her question.

teach.h: TO FIX A HARM, NOT FOR THE TELLING.
teach.b: Naming a fault to fix a harm is different from naming it for the pleasure of the telling. And last, why it's easy: backbiting bonds people. Two friends, a third one absent, and suddenly there's a topic.
The way out is another topic.

how: Muslims are taught to avoid ghibah, speaking of an absent person in a way they would dislike even if it is true, following Sahih Muslim and Qur'an 49:12; scholars allow naming faults for specific needs such as seeking help against injustice.

games.q: what does “the harm of backbiting” mean?
o: spreading lies about someone who isn't there
naming someone's true faults behind their back
criticizing someone directly to their face

games.q: the harm of backbiting — tap the pairs.
p: true, and he'd dislike it said
the flesh of a dead brother
asking for help against a wrong

s: if what you say about someone is true, it isn't backbiting
in Sahih Muslim, if it's true, that's backbiting; if it's false, it's slander.
the Qur'an compares backbiting to eating a dead brother's flesh
"Would one of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother?"
scholars allow no mention of anyone's faults, ever
an-Nawawi and others list exceptions, like seeking help against a wrong.

games.q: a friend says, 'I'm not gossiping, it's true!' by the hadith in Sahih Muslim, what is it?
o: backbiting: true, and he'd dislike it said.
games.why: the Prophet's answer: if it's true, it's backbiting; if it's false, it's slander. truth is the definition, not the defense.

practice: Bring to mind the people you're most likely to talk about, a boss, an in-law, a friend who's been difficult, and one at a time, picture them walking in while you're speaking about them.

Whatever you'd stop saying when they walked in, that's the line. Prepare one way out, a change of subject, a kind word about them, or simply silence, and if you pray, you can ask for help guarding the tongue.

wordCard.voice: The harm of backbiting. Ghibah: mentioning someone with what they'd dislike, even when it's true. When it's false, it's slander. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: backbiting, speaking of someone in their absence with what they'd dislike.

carryVoice: Your line: not behind their backs. If they'd mind hearing it, it can wait. Tomorrow, two roads, and one of them is lying.
